objectives: Recognise tch at the end of taught words such as catch, match, fetch and pitch.
Understand that tch represents one /ch/ phoneme in the taught examples.
Notice the short vowel before final tch in these one-syllable words.
Distinguish the three-letter spelling from three separate spoken sounds.
concepts: A trigraph uses three letters to represent one phoneme.
In taught words, final tch represents /ch/ after a short vowel.
The letters t, c and h are not spoken as three separate sounds in catch.
Some words use final ch instead; learn the taught pattern and exceptions.

definitions.definition: Three letters working together to represent one phoneme.
The smallest sound unit that can distinguish words.
A vowel sound as heard in words such as catch, fetch and pitch.

workedExamples.solution: The final /ch/ sound is written tch.
The final tch represents one /ch/ phoneme after short e.
The final tch represents one /ch/ phoneme after short i.

commonMistakes: Saying separate /t/, /c/ and /h/ sounds at the end.
Writing only ch when the taught word uses tch.
Changing the short vowel when reading the word.
Assuming every English word ending in /ch/ must use tch.
keyTakeaways: In taught words, tch represents one final /ch/ phoneme.
Notice the short vowel before tch.
Read the whole word from left to right.
Learn exceptions and other /ch/ spellings separately.
